James 2
JAYMZ TOO
proper noun
The second chapter of the epistle of James; the great passage on partiality, the royal law, and faith and works.

Biblical Definition

James 2 is the chapter that forbids the respect of persons in the church and shows that a living faith is known by its works. James first rebukes partiality: to honor the rich man in fine apparel and to despise the poor man in vile raiment is to become a judge of evil thoughts and to transgress the royal law, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. He then turns to the great theme—faith without works is dead. A man may say he has faith, but if it has no works, can that faith save him? Faith that does not feed the hungry or clothe the naked is dead, being alone; even the devils believe, and tremble. James points to Abraham, justified when he offered Isaac, and to Rahab, justified when she received the messengers—faith made perfect, that is, shown and proved, by works. As the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also. The dictionary reads James not as contradicting Paul but as completing him: Paul declares that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law, speaking of the ground of justification before God; James declares that the faith which justifies is never alone but is proved living by its fruit. The faith that saves is the faith that works.

Webster 1828 Definition

The second chapter of James; the rebuke of partiality, the royal law of love, and the truth that faith without works is dead—completing, not contradicting, Paul.

Key Scripture

Jas 2:1 — "My brethren, have not the faith of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory, with respect of persons."

Jas 2:8 — "If ye fulfil the royal law according to the scripture, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself, ye do well:"

Jas 2:17 — "Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone."

Jas 2:26 — "For as the body without the spirit is dead, so faith without works is dead also."

Modern Corruption

James 2 is misread as contradicting Paul on justification, and its “works” are claimed for a salvation by works; rightly read, it completes Paul—the faith that justifies is never alone.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The error to answer is the old claim that James contradicts Paul, set against the Reformation’s justification by faith alone, and used to smuggle works back into the ground of salvation. But James and Paul speak to different questions. Paul declares the ground of a sinner’s acceptance before God: a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law, by the imputed righteousness of Christ. James declares the proof of a living faith before men: the faith that truly justifies is never alone, but shows itself living by its works, as Abraham’s faith was proved when he offered Isaac. The justification by faith alone is a justification by a faith that is never alone.

The principle to recover is the wholeness of the Reformation doctrine: faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is a working faith. A bare profession without fruit is dead, being alone—the faith of devils, who believe and tremble. James does not add works to the ground of acceptance; he tests the reality of the faith that lays hold of Christ. The tree is known by its fruit; the faith that saves is the faith that works by love.
